Public GitHub Issue Could Trick GitHub Agentic Workflows Into Leaking Private Repo Data

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 6 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A public issue can trick GitHub Agentic Workflows into leaking the contents of an organization's private repositories, researchers at Noma Security have shown. The attacker needs only to open a normal-looking issue on a public repository, with no stolen credentials and no access to the organization. If that organization has given the agent read access across its repositories, private ones

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-14343")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-14343")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Court Filing Reveals Windows Device ID Helped FBI Trace Alleged Scattered Spider Hacker

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 15 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

U.S. prosecutors linked an alleged Scattered Spider hacker to a break-in at a luxury jewelry retailer using a persistent Windows device ID, according to a newly unsealed federal complaint. Microsoft records tied that ID first to the account the attackers used to keep access during the May 2025 intrusion, then to online accounts prosecutors say belong to 19-year-old Peter Stokes. Stokes is

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Authentication & network activity from court-filing operator proxy IPs · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ngrok / Teleport tunneling binary execution · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ngrok / Teleport tunneling service resolution & egress (Scattered Spider C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Inbound extortion email matching campaign subject string · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ngrok / Teleport tunneling service resolution & egress (Scattered Spider C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/network egress to ngrok and Teleport (teleport.sh) tunneling infrastructure, the exact remote-access tunnels this Scattered Spider cell used to hold access and exfiltrate 77 GB during the May 2025 jewelry-retailer intrusion. Article-specific because both named tools plus the ngrok dashboard domain are cited IOCs. Rationale: ngrok and Teleport are named verbatim in the article as the two tunneling tools; dashboard.ngrok.com is a listed IOC and teleport.sh is confirmed by Darktrace/ReliaQuest as the 77 GB exfil channel. Domain resolution to these services from a corporate endpoint is high-signal where neither tool is sanctioned. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/untangling-the-web-darktraces-investigation-of-scattered-spiders-evolving-tactics • https://reliaquest.com/blog/scattered-spider-attack-analysis-account-compromise/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using ngrok to expose a local dev service
  • IT team piloting Teleport (goteleport.com) for sanctioned bastion/SSH access
  • QA/webhook testing tunnels to ngrok for integration work
  • Security researchers detonating malware in a sandbox that beacons to ngrok
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\dev\", @"\repos\", @"\source\") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-devtunnel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user on the resolving host; confirm whether ngrok/Teleport is sanctioned software for that team. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the tunnel process, and block ngrok/teleport.sh domains at the proxy/firewall; force-reset the involved account and its MFA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for the tunnel binaries (ngrok.exe/tsh.exe), large outbound transfers to amazonaws.com/S3, and help-desk-driven password/MFA resets in the prior 72h.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("ngrok.io","ngrok-free.app","ngrok-free.dev","ngrok.app","ngrok.com","teleport.sh")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("ngrok.io","ngrok-free.app","ngrok-free.dev","ngrok.app","ngrok.com","teleport.sh")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Queries=make_set(DnsQuery,10) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: ngrok or Teleport Tunneling Service DNS Resolution
id: 5f1c3a08-2d94-4c1e-9c7a-8b2e5a4d1f01
description: Detects DNS resolution of ngrok or Teleport (teleport.sh) tunneling infrastructure used by Scattered Spider for C2 and exfiltration.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/court-filing-reveals-windows-device-id.html
  - https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.t1572
  - attack.t1090
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains:
      - 'ngrok.io'
      - 'ngrok-free.app'
      - 'ngrok-free.dev'
      - 'ngrok.app'
      - 'ngrok.com'
      - 'teleport.sh'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*ngrok.io OR *ngrok-free.app OR *ngrok-free.dev OR *ngrok.app OR *ngrok.com OR *teleport.sh OR *Teleport.sh)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(ngrok\.(io|com|app)|ngrok-free\.(app|dev)|teleport\.sh)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("*.ngrok.io","*.ngrok-free.app","*.ngrok-free.dev","*.ngrok.app","dashboard.ngrok.com","*.ngrok.com","teleport.sh","*.teleport.sh")) by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("*.ngrok.io","*.ngrok-free.app","*.ngrok-free.dev","*.ngrok.app","dashboard.ngrok.com","*.ngrok.com","teleport.sh","*.teleport.sh")) by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
ngrok / Teleport tunneling binary execution AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the ngrok agent (ngrok.exe) or Teleport client (tsh.exe / teleport.exe), including tell-tale command lines (ngrok tcp/http/authtoken, tsh login). This is the on-host install/run step of the tunnels used to keep access and stage the 77 GB exfil in the May 2025 intrusion. Rationale: Both ngrok and Teleport are explicitly named; the ngrok.exe agent and Teleport tsh.exe client with their canonical subcommands (tcp/http/authtoken/login) are precise, low-FP execution artifacts distinct from the network pivot in UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://reliaquest.com/blog/scattered-spider-attack-analysis-account-compromise/
ATT&CKT1572 T1219 T1567.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running ngrok.exe for a local webhook demo
  • IT admin using tsh.exe against a sanctioned Teleport cluster
  • CI/CD runner invoking ngrok for ephemeral test tunnels
  • Renamed-but-legit portable ngrok in a user's Downloads for a hackathon
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe") and AccountName in~ ("builduser","ci-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary path, signer, and whether the running user/team is authorized to use ngrok/Teleport; capture the full command line and any authtoken. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host, block the tunnel domains, and revoke/reset the executing account plus its MFA enrollment. 3) Hunt: correlate to preceding help-desk password/MFA resets, outbound transfers to amazonaws.com, and DNS to ngrok/teleport.sh across other hosts sharing the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("ngrok.exe","tsh.exe","teleport.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ngrok tcp","ngrok http","ngrok authtoken","tsh login","teleport.sh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ngrok.exe","tsh.exe","teleport.exe")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ngrok tcp","ngrok http","ngrok authtoken","tsh login","teleport.sh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ngrok or Teleport Tunneling Binary Execution
id: 9a44b7d1-6e03-4f2b-b1a7-0d6c9e2f3a12
description: Detects execution of the ngrok agent or Teleport client used by Scattered Spider for tunneling and cloud exfiltration.

Inbound extortion email matching campaign subject string AIActions on Objectives Medium
Flags inbound email carrying the attackers' distinctive ransom subject line ('WE STOLE THE DATA', typo 'UMMEDIATELY') sent after the retailer blocked the ransomware and evicted them. The misspelling makes this an extremely low-FP string tied to this specific extortion attempt. Rationale: The ransom email subject 'IMPORTANT: WE STOLE THE DATA, CONTACT UMMEDIATELY [sic]' is quoted verbatim in the article; the 'UMMEDIATELY' misspelling is a near-unique string, so a subject match is high-precision. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — the signal lives only in mail telemetry (Defender EmailEvents / Splunk Email datamodel), which has no clean equivalent in those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/court-filing-reveals-windows-device-id.html • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/07/windows-is-watching-anti-piracy-tool-fingers-scattered-spider-suspect/5267953
ATT&CKT1657 T1486
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal phishing-simulation exercise reusing the leaked subject line
  • Threat-intel briefing or news forward that quotes the ransom subject in the body/subject
  • Analyst mailing the sample subject to a shared mailbox for triage
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryAction != "Blocked" | where SenderFromDomain !endswith "phishsim.contoso.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full message (sender, headers, SenderIPv4, any crypto wallet / $8M demand) and confirm it is a genuine external extortion note, not a sim or forward. 2) Contain: quarantine the message tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, preserve it for IR/legal, and notify incident command — a received extortion note implies data was already staged/taken. 3) Hunt: work backwards for the breach — prior ngrok/Teleport tunnels, 77 GB-class transfers to Amazon S3, and help-desk resets on privileged accounts.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject has_any ("WE STOLE THE DATA","UMMEDIATELY","CONTACT UMMEDIATELY")
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderIPv4, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject has_any ("WE STOLE THE DATA","UMMEDIATELY","CONTACT UMMEDIATELY")
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderIPv4, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.subject="*WE STOLE THE DATA*" OR All_Email.subject="*UMMEDIATELY*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.subject="*WE STOLE THE DATA*" OR All_Email.subject="*UMMEDIATELY*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Authentication & network activity from court-filing operator proxy IPs AIExploitation Medium
Matches sign-ins and outbound connections against the twelve VPN/proxy IPs from the unsealed complaint that the operator used to reach the ngrok signup page and the retailer's site. Use as an IOC sweep for the same infrastructure across the estate, including CloudTrail source IPs for the S3 exfil. Rationale: The twelve proxy IPs are pre-extracted IOCs from the complaint that the device repeatedly surfaced on (ngrok signup, retailer access). They are shared commercial-VPN ranges (mostly 146.70.x M247/DataPacket), hence Medium confidence — a hit warrants investigation but not blind blocking. CloudTrail sweep is included because exfil went to Amazon S3, so these source IPs may appear on PutObject calls. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/court-filing-reveals-windows-device-id.html • https://gbhackers.com/windows-device-track-scattered-spider-hacking-group-member/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1090
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee legitimately using the same commercial VPN provider (Mullvad/M247 shared egress) for privacy
  • Traveling user routed through a VPN concentrator on an overlapping IP
  • Threat-intel scanner or researcher pivoting from the same VPN range
  • IP re-allocated to a benign tenant since the May 2025 activity (shared-IP staleness)
Suppression filter
| where ResultType == 0 and UserAgent !has "Mullvad" | where AppDisplayName in~ ("Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Azure Active Directory PowerShell") == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm the account, app, and whether the sign-in succeeded; check if the user has any business reason to use that VPN and whether the auth was MFA-satisfied. 2) Contain: for successful privileged sign-ins, revoke sessions, reset credentials + MFA, and add the IPs to a monitored/blocked list (block cautiously — shared VPN). 3) Hunt: from any matched account pivot to ngrok/Teleport execution, S3 uploads, and help-desk reset events; sweep CloudTrail for these IPs on S3/IAM actions.
let iocIPs = dynamic(["146.70.134.82","79.127.222.213","146.70.126.237","193.32.127.231","146.70.126.215","138.199.6.242","46.19.136.247","138.199.6.216","193.32.248.138","146.70.126.183","23.234.88.97","146.70.134.23"]);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where IPAddress in (iocIPs)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Application, ErrorCode, Country, City, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

logsource:

detection:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:

       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental

references:

Writer AI Flaw Could Let Agent Previews Leak Session Tokens Across Tenants

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 5 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched critical session isolation vulnerability in Writer, an enterprise generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform, that could result in cross-tenant compromise. The one-click vulnerability has been codenamed WriteOut by the Sand Security Research team. "An outsider could go from having no access to taking over any Writer AI

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1539 T1555.003
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Exploitation
Detected

Detected

Detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

DeviceRegistryEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,

ImRegistryEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

EGroupware CVE-2026-27823 arbitrary file read via importexport download path traversal AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the EGroupware importexport export handler carrying a traversal-laden _filename parameter. This is the arbitrary-file-read primitive attackers use to exfiltrate a valid header.inc.php before overwriting it for RCE — article-specific because it pins the exact vulnerable menuaction and parameter. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable menuaction 'importexport.importexport_export_ui.download' plus a path-traversal _filename token straight from the advisory's PoC URL — the pair is not something benign EGroupware traffic produces. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p • https://www.cvedetails.com/vulnerability-list/vendor_id-2373/Egroupware.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing EGroupware with traversal templates
  • Internal pentest or red-team validation of CVE-2026-27823
  • Security researcher testing after patch to confirm remediation
  • WAF in monitor-mode logging blocked-then-passed requests
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the HTTP status — a 200 with a non-trivial response body means the file read succeeded; extract SrcIpAddr and check whether _filename resolved to header.inc.php or another sensitive file. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm EGroupware is patched (>= 26.2.20260224 / >= 23.1.20260224); disable user self-registration if enabled. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for subsequent POST uploads to the SmallPart media recorder and for any modification of header.inc.php on the host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "menuaction=importexport.importexport_export_ui.download"
| where Url has_any ("_filename=../", "_filename=..%2f", "%2e%2e%2f", "..%5c", "header.inc.php")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware header.inc.php overwritten by web process (CVE-2026-27823 RCE persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects the web/PHP runtime writing or modifying header.inc.php — EGroupware's core bootstrap config, which is normally only written during setup. In CVE-2026-27823 the auth-bypass file-write primitive overwrites this file with attacker PHP to achieve RCE on restart/OPcache expiry. Rationale: header.inc.php is EGroupware's bootstrap config; a write to it by php/php-fpm/apache at runtime (not during setup) is the exact RCE persistence artifact named in the advisory. Filename + web-process parent make it very high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate EGroupware setup/reconfiguration wizard writing header.inc.php
  • Admin editing config via the setup UI after an upgrade
  • Automated deployment/config-management (Ansible/Puppet) templating header.inc.php — but that runs as a deploy user, not php-fpm
  • Package upgrade regenerating the config file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup","cli.php","doctrine") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Diff the new header.inc.php against a known-good copy; look for injected PHP (system/exec/passthru, base64 blobs, added functions) beyond the expected config array. 2) CONTAIN: Restore header.inc.php from backup, kill the php-fpm/apache workers, and take the host off the network if injected code is present. 3) HUNT: Search DeviceProcessEvents for php-fpm/apache spawning shells or network tools, and review web logs for the preceding SmallPart ajax_upload POST and importexport file-read that seeded the attack.

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/www","/usr/share/egroupware")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName

EGroupware web runtime (php-fpm/apache) spawning a shell or network tool — CVE-2026-27823 RCE execution AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the PHP/web server process spawning interactive shells or download utilities, the observable execution stage once CVE-2026-27823's poisoned header.inc.php runs. Article-specific because EGroupware executes as www-data under php-fpm/apache, so shell children of that process are anomalous. Rationale: The advisory states EGroupware runs as www-data under the web server and achieves RCE via header.inc.php; a php-fpm/apache parent spawning a shell or curl/wget is the direct execution signature of that RCE, keyed on the runtime's own process names. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EGroupware cron/async jobs invoking php CLI that shells out (e.g. mail delivery, LDAP sync)
  • Server monitoring plugins run under the web user calling id/uname/whoami
  • ImageMagick/document-conversion features legitimately calling helper binaries
  • Deployment hooks or health-checks executed by the web process during restart
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","/tmp/","http://","https://","/dev/tcp","base64","-i")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell one-liners, curl|bash to external IPs, or recon (id;uname -a) are true-positive; a known EGroupware maintenance task is benign. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, capture the php-fpm/apache process tree, and rotate EGroupware admin/setup credentials (advisory notes setup-password modification as an alternative impact). 3) HUNT: Correlate back to the header.inc.php write and the importexport file-read/SmallPart upload from the same host/IP, and scan for outbound C2 from the web process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","whoami","id","uname")

ImProcessCreate

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Non-virtualization process accessing /dev/kvm on KVM host (Januscape CVE-2026-53359 LPE precursor) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts local processes that open or reference /dev/kvm on a hypervisor host while NOT being part of the legitimate virtualization stack (qemu/libvirt/firecracker/etc.). On RHEL and other distros where /dev/kvm is world-writable, an unprivileged local user can drive the CVE-2026-53359 shadow-MMU use-after-free through this device to gain root — so an unexpected opener is the earliest host-side signal of exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete device path (/dev/kvm) and the explicit RHEL world-writable-device LPE condition; the virtualization-stack allowlist keeps qemu/libvirt/firecracker noise out so a residual hit is an unexpected opener. Cross-checked TheHackerNews and the oss-security disclosure which name kvm_mmu_get_child_sp() and confirm the unprivileged /dev/kvm path. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/16-year-old-linux-kvm-flaw-lets-guest.html • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/06/7 • https://securityonline.info/januscape-kvm-escape-cve-2026-53359-poc/
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Lightweight VMMs not on the allowlist (e.g. cloud-hypervisor forks, gVisor/runsc, Weston/Android emulators) legitimately opening /dev/kvm
  • Capability probes: kvm-ok, virt-host-validate, systemd-detect-virt run by config-management (Ansible/Puppet)
  • CI runners that spin nested KVM for kernel/image builds
  • Container runtimes with KVM passthrough (Kata, Firecracker under containerd) invoked by a non-listed wrapper
  • GPU/PCI-passthrough tooling that touches /dev/kvm during device setup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","python3","runsc","containerd","containerd-shim") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("open","O_RDWR")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process image, parent, and account — is it a known VMM/admin tool, and is the account unprivileged? Confirm whether the host runs multi-tenant guests and whether /dev/kvm is world-writable (stat /dev/kvm). 2) Contain: if the opener is unexpected and non-service, isolate the host from the guest fleet, tighten /dev/kvm to root/kvm group (chmod 660, kvm group), and snapshot the process/binary for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same account/binary for prior compilations, downloads of Januscape/kvmCTF PoC artifacts, and correlate with UC-2 (host kernel panic) and UC-3 (unpatched kernel missing commit 81ccda30b4e8).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/dev/kvm"
| where FileName !in~ ("qemu-system-x86_64","qemu-system-i386","qemu-kvm","qemu","libvirtd","virtqemud","cloud-hypervisor","firecracker","crosvm","kata-runtime","virt-host-validate","kvm-ok")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("libvirtd","virtqemud","systemd")
| where AccountName !in~ ("root","libvirt-qemu","qemu")   // world-writable /dev/kvm path is exploited by UNPRIVILEGED users
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/dev/kvm"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("type=SYSCALL","type=PATH","type=EXECVE","exe=")   // auditd records touching the device node
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("qemu","libvirt","cloud-hypervisor","firecracker","crosvm","kata","virt-host-validate","kvm-ok"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-virtualization process accessing /dev/kvm (Januscape CVE-2026-53359 LPE precursor)
id: 6b1e9d2a-7c34-4f81-9a2e-0d4c53359a01
description: Detects a process other than the known virtualization stack opening the /dev/kvm device node, the local-privesc entry point for CVE-2026-53359 on hosts where /dev/kvm is world-writable.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/linux/new-januscape-linux-kernel-flaw-allows-vm-escape-on-intel-amd-devices/
  - https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/06/7
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1611
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename: '/dev/kvm'
  filter:
    Image:
      - '*/qemu*'
      - '*/libvirtd'
      - '*/virtqemud'
      - '*/cloud-hypervisor'
      - '*/firecracker'
      - '*/crosvm'
      - '*/kata-runtime'
      - '*/virt-host-validate'
      - '*/kvm-ok'
  condition: selection and not filter
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @process.command_line:*/dev/kvm* -@process.name:(qemu* OR libvirt* OR cloud-hypervisor OR firecracker OR crosvm OR kata* OR virt-host-validate OR kvm-ok)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/\/dev\/kvm$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/(qemu|libvirt|cloud-hypervisor|firecracker|crosvm|kata|virt-host-validate|kvm-ok)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

KVM/x86 hosts unpatched for Januscape CVE-2026-53359 and chained Dirty Frag CVEs AIExploitation High
Surfaces Linux hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-53359 and the Dirty Frag chain (CVE-2026-43284 xfrm-ESP, CVE-2026-43500 RxRPC) that the researcher noted can be combined for full compromise without guest root. This is the posture pivot that scopes which multi-tenant KVM hosts still need patch commit 81ccda30b4e8, prioritizing the response for UC-1 and UC-2. Rationale: Uses the three concrete CVE IDs from the article (Januscape plus the explicitly-named Dirty Frag chain the author says can be combined for full compromise) against vuln-management telemetry; deterministic CVE match makes this a clean prioritization list rather than a behavioral guess. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/16-year-old-linux-kvm-flaw-lets-guest.html • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/06/7
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts flagged by scanner metadata lag after patch (commit 81ccda30b4e8) is applied but package version string unchanged
  • Non-hypervisor Linux hosts (no KVM guests) reported vulnerable to the kernel CVE but not actually exposing the guest-to-host surface
  • Backported vendor kernels where the scanner mis-maps the fixed version
  • Containers/appliances inheriting the host kernel double-counted per instance
  • Air-gapped or decommissioned hosts still in the asset inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank returned hosts by whether they run untrusted/multi-tenant guests and by internet exposure; verify true state with `git log --oneline | grep 81ccda30b4e8`-equivalent kernel version check. 2) Contain: for confirmed-vulnerable multi-tenant hosts, schedule emergency kernel patching/live-patch and, as interim mitigation, restrict /dev/kvm permissions and limit guest provisioning. 3) Hunt: on any host still unpatched, correlate against UC-1 (/dev/kvm access) and UC-2 (kernel panic) to determine whether exposure has already been exercised.

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
